headline: Phone scam warning: callers impersonating Chief Lindstrom
summary: South Windsor Police warn that callers impersonating Chief Lindstrom told a resident they were a victim of identity theft and asked for personal identifying information. The department never asks for personal identifying information by phone.
body: Good morning #SW06074.  Yesterday, a citizen received a phone call from someone claiming to be Chief Lindstrom; the caller ID showed the police department's main phone number, 860-644-2551.  The caller claimed the citizen was a victim of identity theft and needed to provide personal identifying information to address the issue.  Thankfully, the citizen recognized this as a scam, hung up, and came to the PD lobby to file a report.

As a reminder, police department employees will never contact citizens and ask for personal identifying information.  If you believe you may be subject to a scam, hang up the phone immediately, do not provide the caller with any information, and contact the police department if personal identifying information (DOB, SSN, etc.) was given so a report can be filed and the appropriate steps can be taken to protect your identity.

headline: 69-home senior community plan faces neighbors' backlash at hearing
summary: The Planning and Zoning Commission heard the 69-home 55-plus community proposed for 100 Oakland Road on Tuesday, Nov. 10. The hearing ran past 10:30 p.m. and was continued to a special public hearing on Tuesday, Dec. 1, with no vote taken.
body: The proposed Estates at 100 Oakland is a 69-home community for residents 55 and older, on 32.53 acres at 15 Petersen Way, 50 Darlene Drive, and 80, 90 and 100 Oakland Road. The developer is Jim Newbury, president of Bestech Inc. of Connecticut.
The homes would be single-story, two to three bedrooms, 1,200 to 2,400 square feet. Eleven of the 69 homes would be sold at affordable prices, developer Jim Newbury said.

The Planning and Zoning Commission held a public hearing on the site-design application (26-29P) on Tuesday, November 10. Eight neighbors spoke against the plan or raised concerns. At 10:30 p.m., the commission voted unanimously to continue the public hearing to a special meeting on Tuesday, December 1, 2026. No vote was taken on the application.

headline: Homeowner praised after McGrath Road kitchen fire
summary: A stovetop fire on McGrath Road on Thursday, Nov. 12, spread to the cabinets above and was quickly extinguished. The homeowner evacuated the family, called 911 and turned off the burner.
body: South Windsor firefighters were dispatched at 7:03 p.m. on Thursday, November 12, to a stove fire on McGrath Road.
The homeowner found a pan of cooking oil on fire, evacuated the family, called 911 and turned off the burner. The fire extended from the stovetop to the cabinets above and was quickly extinguished.
Firefighters credited the homeowner for calling 911 with accurate information and for not trying to carry the burning pan outside.

headline: South Windsor rejects religious campus zoning changes
summary: The Planning and Zoning Commission voted 4-3 on Oct. 27 to reject a zoning-text change that would have allowed religious campuses with housing in residential zones. The proposal was for a campus at 401 King Street.
body: The Planning and Zoning Commission voted 4-3 on Tuesday, October 27, against a zoning-text amendment that would have allowed religious campuses in residential zones.

The Golden Lampstand Association proposed a religious campus at 401 King Street, with a ministry building, an eight-room retreat center, and housing for current and retired clergy and returning missionaries, up to 12 units, with an affordability component, with up to 15 percent building coverage and 50 percent impervious surface.
Commissioners Kilburn, Kupchunos, Welch and Foley voted against the change. Commissioners Lopez and Dexter and Chair Bernstein voted in favor.

headline: New high school plan: $365-385 million, referendum March 2, 2027
summary: The Board of Education proposes a new high school on the Brookfield Street fairgrounds site, at a preliminary cost of $365-385 million, with a referendum on March 2, 2027, and an opening in August 2032.
body: The Board of Education proposes building a new high school on town-owned parcels on Brookfield Street, known as the Wapping Fair and John J. Mitchell Fairgrounds. Fairgrounds activities would move to town-owned Priest Farm. Eight other properties were evaluated and ruled out.

The preliminary cost is $365-385 million. State support would be about $271-286 million under special legislation, Public Act 26-68, at a 74.17 percent reimbursement rate, with a local share of 25.83 percent of eligible costs. The reimbursement could rise to 82.55 percent, about $30 million more, if additional increases are approved after the referendum. That increase is not guaranteed, because the State will not formally approve it until after the referendum.
The school would be about 350,000 to 375,000 square feet, for a highest projected enrollment of about 1,850 students.
A referendum is scheduled for March 2, 2027. The state grant application is due no later than June 30, 2027. The school would open in August 2032, for the 2032-33 school year.

The current high school would become the permanent home for Parks and Recreation, plus Human Services, Youth and Family Services, and Teen Center offices, avoiding $50-80 million in proposed new Parks and Recreation facility costs.
The tax impact has not yet been published. The Town Manager's office will calculate it once the total cost is finalized.

headline: Flock cameras: Town Council voted to end the contract
summary: On Oct. 5, 2026, the Town Council voted 6-3 to terminate the Flock camera contract, shut off the cameras, remove them within 60 days, and purge South Windsor data. Another public hearing would be required before reinstalling cameras.
body: South Windsor police began using Flock automated license plate reader cameras in April 2025. The rollout drew widespread concern from residents about how the technology was evaluated and introduced. The cameras capture rear plate images with location, date and time.

After a public debate, the Town Council voted 6-3 on October 5, 2026, to terminate the Flock contract, shut off the cameras, remove them within 60 days, and purge South Windsor data. Another public hearing would be required before cameras could be reinstalled.
The cameras are to be removed by about December 4, 2026, 60 days after the vote.

Police Chief Kristian Lindstrom has said searches require an offense type, a case number and a reason, and that South Windsor data is shared only within Connecticut, not with federal law enforcement. The ACLU and residents have raised data-protection concerns.

headline: Crumbling foundations: claims help continues, deadline June 30, 2030
summary: Help remains available for South Windsor homeowners with crumbling foundations. The Connecticut Foundations Solutions Indemnity Company will not accept new claims after June 30, 2030.
body: Crumbling foundations remain a major issue for South Windsor homeowners. The Connecticut Foundations Solutions Indemnity Company (CFSIC) and the Capitol Region Council of Governments prepared a dedicated South Windsor landing page and Resource Guide.
More than 2,500 applications have been received overall, many from South Windsor, and more than $200 million has been spent helping families.
CFSIC will not accept new claims after June 30, 2030. That date is the deadline for new claims.
Homeowners can contact CFSIC at info@crumblingfoundations.org or 844-763-1207, the Superintendent's Office at 860-487-0000, or CRCOG at 860-724-4292.
